issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette: Forty-four-year-old Dat Nguyen was walking home from his night shift at the county hospital when the mugging occurred. The violence was sudden, leaving a heavy pressure across his ribs and a sharp, grinding ache in his left shoulder where the man's elbow had driven into him. He remembered the attacker's face not as a continuous scene but as a series of sharp, static frames: the glint of the knife, the wide eyes, the tension in the jaw. When the memory returns, he feels physical pain in the same parts of his body as during the event, the old pressure and ache surfacing without warning. His memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images, and remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in his mind. Over the next several weeks, those photographs began to appear alongside his daily routine. He had come to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore, that there is something about him that made the event happen, and that he carries a quiet hopelessness alongside his daily tasks. By the third month, his environment and his habits had aligned into a steady pattern of observation. At the nurse's station, he never sat in the open aisles. He always chooses where to sit based on how safe or protected he feels, tucking his chair against the wall or near the corner partition so he could brace against passing equipment. He kept the hallway mirrors within his line of sight, keep checking mirrors to ensure his own reflection was steady and unthreatened. His mind never rested; he kept mind occupied all the time, mentally tallying floor tiles, reciting medication dosages, and tracking the rhythmic beeping of the cardiac monitor. He constantly scans environment for signs of threat, his eyes moving toward doorways, elevators, and the central supply carts. When he walks to his car after a shift, he frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, his shoulders held tight, his steps measured. These habits have accumulated quietly over months. His wife has noticed how he lingers in the living room chair angled toward the street, and at work he avoids the sudden movement of rolling carts, holding his body ready. He held his sleep problems alongside his vigilance, lying in bed for hours, trouble falling or staying asleep because the quiet room felt dangerously exposed. He did not attribute his waking hours to his nights, nor his scanning to his seating; these states simply coexisted in his life, each present and distinct. What finally brought Dat to seek help was the way the fear had settled into his routine and his bed. He lay awake for hours, the photographs of the mugging surfacing without warning, pressing against his ribs and shoulder, and he sat up, certain that the danger remained. He was most afraid of losing the careful balance he had built, of the slow accumulation of waiting that seemed to fill his days. What he hoped for was not to forget the event, but to understand why it had happened to him, and to find a way to move through the hospital, his car, and his home without bracing for impact.
